To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the critical density separating hadronic matter (HM) from the mixed phase (MP) of quark and hadronic matter is very low for nuclei with a low value of $Z/A$, and (ii) the value of the critical density is sensitive to the equation of state (EoS) of HM.

the critical density for quark-hadron transition is strongly suppressed in nuclei with $Z/A \simeq $ 0.4, which opens the possibility to test the Witten-Bodeker hypothesis on quark matter stability using ground-based experiments, and that the transition density is very similar to the density at saturation in symmetric nuclear matter, which opens a possibility to test this hypothesis in heavy-ion collisions.

(i) the quark deconfinement density decreases with increasing neutron excess; (ii) the critical density is very low for nuclei with $Z/A \simeq 0.3$; (iii) the critical density for neutron stars is much higher than that for nuclei with the same neutron excess.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the isospin dependence of quark-hadronic phase transitions.
a new aspect of the problem of the existence of strange quark stars: the dependence of the transition density from nuclear matter to quark matter on the isospin asymmetry.
the study of the isospin dependence of quark deconfinement.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in general, the critical quark-hadron transition density is a function of $Z/A$.
the critical density for the onset of the quark phase is very small and it depends strongly on the isospin asymmetry of the system.
the critical quark deconfinement density is a strong function of $Z/A$.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the critical density of quark deconfinement drops dramatically with the isospin content of the system.
the quark-deconﬁnement phase transition is a neutron star phenomenon.
, for $Z \leq 40$, the Witten-Boden hypothesis can be verified in ground-based experiments.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the critical density is strongly isospin-dependent, and the critical isospin asymmetry is very small, $\Delta \alpha \equiv \alpha_c - \alpha_0 \sim 0.01$--0.03.
the critical density is a strong function of the isospin asymmetry of nuclear matter, and this dependence is very model-independent.
the critical density for the quark-hadron phase transition is strongly dependent on the isospin asymmetry of the system.
